title: Recording, mixing: Cold Turkey, Don’t Worry Kyoko by Plastic Ono Band | 1971
content:
Record Plant, New York City
Producers: John Lennon, Yoko Ono, Phil Spector
Engineers: Roy Cicala, Jack Douglas

John Lennon and Yoko Ono mixed two live recordings from 1969 on 31 October 1971.

The Plastic Ono Band had performed at a benefit concert on 15 December 1969 for the charity Unicef, at the Lyceum Ballroom in central London. The event was titled Peace For Christmas.

The line-up, playing before a huge “War is over” backdrop, was: Lennon, George Harrison, Eric Clapton and Delaney Bramlett (guitars, with Clapton playing Rocky, Harrison’s psychedelic Fender Stratocaster); Ono (vocals); Bonnie Bramlett (tambourine); Alan White and Jim Gordon (drums); Billy Preston (organ); Klaus Voormann (bass guitar); Bobby Keys (saxophone); and Jim Price (trumpet). Lennon later referred to it as the Plastic Ono Supergroup.

I thought it was fantastic. I was really into it. We were doing the show and George and Bonnie and Delaney, Billy Preston and all that crowd turned up. They’d just come back from Sweden and George had been playing invisible man in Bonnie and Delaney’s band, which Eric Clapton had been doing, to get the pressure off being the famous Eric and the famous George. They became the guitarists in this and they all turned up, and it was again like the concert in Toronto. I said, ‘Will you come on?’ They said, ‘Well, what are you going to play?’ I said, ‘Listen, we’re going to do probably a blues… or Cold Turkey, which is three chords, and Eric knew that.’ And Don’t Worry Kyoko, which was Yoko’s, which has three chords and a riff. I said, ‘Once we get on to Yoko’s riff, just keep hitting it.’
John Lennon

They performed just two songs: the Plastic Ono Band’s current single ‘Cold Turkey’, and its b-side ‘Don’t Worry Kyoko (Mummy’s Only Looking For Her Hand In The Snow)’. The first song lasted for nearly seven minutes, and was introduced by Lennon with the words: “We’d like to do a number. This song’s about pain.”

‘Don’t Worry Kyoko’ lasted for around 40 minutes, though it was trimmed to 15 minutes for the album release. Emerick was forced to change tape reels midway through, and at least three edits are evident in the released version. It featured the guitarists and horns locked in various grooves and riffs as Ono wailed over the top.

The performance was recorded on four-track tape by Geoff Emerick, with Peter Bown and John Kurlander engineering. It was mixed two days later, and again on this day.

The multitrack recordings were transferred to 16-track tape at the beginning of this session. Lennon then overdubbed more lead vocals onto ‘Cold Turkey’, and Voormann and Nicky Hopkins added more bass guitar and electric piano respectively.

Voormann also added a new bass part to ‘Don’t Worry Kyoko’, after which both song were mixed in mono and stereo. The recordings were released on a bonus disc with the 1972 album Some Time In New York City.
